blocks.text: The ID generation — a core design decision
We need a short, unique, non-guessable code.

blocks.code:
id = global_counter++
code = base62(id)

items.text: Pros: shortest possible code, trivially unique.
Cons: **sequential → guessable**. And a global counter is a serialization bottleneck

blocks.code: code = base62(random 7 bytes)   → 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations

items.text: Pros: unguessable, no coordination, no collision retry needed (or very rare).
Cons: slightly longer, collisions possible (retry on unique-constraint violation).

blocks.code: code = base62(sha256(url)[:8])

items.text: Pros: deterministic, idempotent (the same URL always gets the same code) — no storage needed
Cons: the same URL always maps to the same code (some users want multiple links to the same

blocks.text: target), and it's guessable if the attacker knows the target.
**Decision:** Option B (random 7-char Base62), with a **unique constraint** on the code as the collision guard. Store the mapping in Postgres.
**Base62 detail:** 62^7 = 3.52 trillion; at 100M links/year you'd need 28 years to exhaust half the space. Good. Some systems use 8 chars for headroom.
At 35k peak RPS with ~0.003 writes/sec, we have an extreme read:write ratio (~10 million : 1).
**Cache sizing:** 1B clicks/day, but how many *distinct* links are hot? A Zipfian distribution:

items.text: Top 1% of links (1M links) → ~50% of clicks.

blocks.text: Redis at 500 bytes/entry × 100M links = 50 GB. That fits on one big instance or a small cluster. **But** if we cache every link forever, the cache is 50 GB and hit rate is only proportional to the traffic distribution. Better: **cache only the hot links** (LRU with a big keyspace) — the top 10% of links will be almost entirely in cache, giving a ~95-99% hit rate.
**Should we use a redirect (302) or a forward (301)?**

items.text: **302 (temporary):** the browser doesn't cache; every click hits your server. Accurate analytics.
**301 (permanent):** the browser caches the mapping and **never asks you again** — great for

blocks.text: latency and cost, but your analytics become wildly inaccurate and you can't change or expire the link.
**Decision:** 302 by default; offer 301 as an opt-in for links that never expire. This is a real product trade-off most candidates miss.
We have ~70 ms of headroom — enough to afford a signed-URL signature check, rate limiting, and analytics emission inline. But if we added a DB lookup on the miss path, we'd blow it.

sections.title: The core trade-off: fan-out on write vs. fan-out on read

blocks.text: This is *the* question in feed design. There are three options:
When a user posts, push the post into every follower's feed (at scale, into a Redis list per user).

rows: Reads are a **single Redis read** — extremely fast (p99 ~10 ms)
**Write amplification**: a post by a user with 1M followers = 1M pushes
**Celebrity problem**: a celebrity post does millions of writes
Unfollowed users still have stale posts until cleaned up

blocks.text: Store each user's own posts. On a feed request, query the posts of everyone the user follows and merge.
Option C: Hybrid (what real systems do)

rows: **Fan-out on write** into a Redis sorted set
**Fan-out on read** — merge their recent posts at request time
Pull from a precomputed "celebrity posts" list, merged separately

blocks.text: **Decision: hybrid.** This is the answer that shows real experience. Explain the threshold and why: below it, write amplification is cheap and reads are instant; above it, write amplification is ruinous.

-- Source of truth for posts
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id          bigint PRIMARY KEY,        -- snowflake
  author_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  content     text,
  media_ids   uuid[],
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  like_count  int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  comment_count int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  deleted_at  timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX ON posts (author_id, created_at DESC);

-- Follow graph (sharded by follower_id)
CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id uuid NOT NULL,
  followee_id uuid NOT NULL,
  created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON follows (followee_id);   -- for "who follows me" / follower counts

blocks.text: **Snowflake IDs** for post IDs: time-ordered (good index locality), unique across shards, no central coordination.

items.text: `ZADD feed:{u} <ts> <post_id>` on fan-out write.
Read: `ZREVRANGE feed:{u} 0 19` → the 20 most recent.
**Cap the size**: `ZREMRANGEBYRANK feed:{u} 0 -1001` (keep the last 1000). Otherwise it grows
Trimming must happen after each write (or on a schedule).

blocks.text: **Problem:** the feed only contains posts *from* people you follow, but fan-out-on-write means posts are pushed to followers at post time. If you unfollow someone, their posts remain in your feed until trimmed. **Fix:** on unfollow, remove that followee's recent posts from the feed (or filter at read time by checking the follow graph — expensive). Real systems do the former, or accept the staleness and filter at read time for correctness-critical cases.
Pure recency ("show me the newest") is simple but bad. Real feeds rank by engagement:

blocks.code:
score = w1·recency_decay + w2·log(likes + comments + shares + 1)
                + w3·affinity(author, user) + w4·author_quality

items.text: **Recency decay**: `exp(-age / half_life)` or `1 / (age_hours + 2)^1.5` (Reddit/HN style).
**Engagement**: log-scaled (a post with 10 likes ≠ 10x a post with 1 like).
**Affinity**: how much the user interacts with that author.
**Diversity/author caps**: no more than N posts from one author in a row (a known engagement
**ML ranking** at scale (a trained model over hundreds of features), with exploration (epsilon-greedy

blocks.text: or Thompson sampling) to avoid a filter bubble.
**Time window:** a feed typically shows posts from the **last 3-7 days**. After that, posts drop out of the "feed" and live in the profile.

sections.title: The core problem: fan-out at scale

blocks.text: A user with 1M followers who posts → 1M notifications. That's the "celebrity notification" problem.

rows: At event time, write a notification row per recipient
Write cost = O(followers). A celebrity post = 1M writes.
Store one row per event; the recipient computes their notifications at read time
Read cost = O(events to scan). Simple writes.

blocks.text: **2. Throttling / digesting.** "Don't notify me about every like." Aggregate:

blocks.code:
likes: aggregate for 1 hour → "You have 47 new likes" (or omit below a threshold)
comments: always immediate (higher value)

blocks.text: **3. Deduplication.** The same event must not produce two notifications. Use an **idempotency key**: `event_id + recipient_id + channel`. A unique constraint in the DB (or a Redis SET) prevents duplicates. Essential because the pipeline is at-least-once.

The bottleneck becomes **provider rate limits** and the **SMS cost**. Add a dedicated queue per channel with per-provider concurrency limits. Consider pulling the "recipient resolution" into a separate service.

**Find the load-bearing decision** in each design: - Shortener: the read:write ratio → caching strategy. - Feed: the fan-out trade-off → the hybrid strategy. - Notifications: the recipient resolution → the hybrid + batching.
